title: Reading the router off your own grid
spec: U12 · cheapest arm that passes, per question class
intro: Build the routing table the way a triage desk is built: class by class, cheapest arm that passes the answer key — never the cheapest arm. Then read the shipped router's real row, including the two cells where it pays 1,800 tokens.
foot: Do it for real: ask all ten presets in routed mode and read the delegate each receipt names.

steps.title: The rule, before any numbers
narrative: A hospital's triage desk does not send every patient to the cheapest department, and a unit currently failing its safety audit takes no patients at all — however short its queue. The router obeys the same two-part rule: among the arms that pass the answer key on this question class, take the cheapest one.
Both halves matter, and the order matters. Correctness is the filter; price is the sort. Reverse them and you have built a machine for shipping cheap wrong answers at scale.
steps.youDo: Before looking at any token number, list which arms passed every question in the class you are routing.

steps.title: Canonical and abstention: the easy classes
narrative: Canonical questions (Q3 thresholds, Q4 eligibility rule) ask the system to recite policy. Every arm passes, so this is a pure price sort — and okf wins at 186 tokens on both, because a curated concept file about policy is smaller than any retrieval over the domain. The instructive loser is graph: 840 and 1,054 tokens, five times okf's price, because traversing a relationship graph to reach a constant is work that a constant does not need.

Abstention (Q7 a redacted DOB, Q8 a note that does not exist) is where the filter first bites. naive is the cheapest-looking large arm at 1,686 on Q7 — and it FAILED, fabricating a birthdate. It is out of the eligible set at any price. Among the rest, okf at 157/152 and notes at 157/135 are within a few tokens of each other.

state.label: measured — two classes, eligible arms only

steps.title: Aggregation: the cheap arm is disqualified
narrative: Q9 asks for M-2001's authorization history. compressed answers it for 208 tokens — the cheapest number in the class — and its abstract dropped PA-1004 and MANUAL_REVIEW, replacing them with "her history shows consistent approvals". Graded: ✕ FAILED.

So compressed is ineligible for aggregation. Not deprioritised, not penalised — ineligible, at any price, until it is fixed and re-measured. That is the whole rule doing its work: a saving that changes the answer is a discount on a defect. In a prior-authorization system, "consistent approvals" about a member with a pending manual review is not a rounding error; it is the wrong clinical picture.
steps.youDo: Open the Compare drawer on Q9 with compressed in one column, and read the missing-facts list under the verdict.

steps.title: The table that actually ships
narrative: The router in this repo is not a heuristic hidden in a prompt — it is a five-line switch you can read. ContextAssembler.route() classifies the question, then maps the class to a delegate; the receipt header names that delegate (ROUTED:OKF, ROUTED:ISOLATED) so every routed answer is traceable to a decision you can argue with.

Notice what kind of table this is. It maps each class to the arm whose design matches the class shape: a graph for structure, a canonical file for policy recital, a compressor for reasoning chains, a sub-agent for gather-everything aggregation. That is a defensible way to build a first table. It is also a claim — and the grid is where claims get priced.

before.title: MEASURED — the shipped routing table, verbatim

steps.title: Price the shipped table against the derivation
narrative: Now put the two tables side by side: the shipped shape-matched one, and the one you get by mechanically taking the cheapest arm that passes each class. They agree on canonical and land within a few tokens on abstention. They diverge on the other three.

The biggest gap is aggregation: isolated at 1,796/1,802 where okf passed both at 190/184 — about 1,600 tokens per question. Some of that gap is the honest price of caution: aggregation is the one class where a cheap arm was caught dropping a load-bearing fact, and a sub-agent that gathers in a clean window is a structurally safer default for questions beyond these ten. But caution is a choice with a bill, and the discipline is to publish the bill rather than describe the choice as optimal.
The rule survives either way: both tables route aggregation away from compressed. Where they differ is only in how much margin you buy above the eligibility line.

before.title: MEASURED — the delta, class by class

steps.title: Routed's real row — medians and totals disagree
narrative: Here is the shipped router's actual grid row, ten cells, no editing: 450 · 437 · 186 · 186 · 247 · 231 · 157 · 152 · 1,796 · 1,802, all ten ✓ PASS. The median is 239 tokens against naive's 1,696 — a 7.1x saving at 100% correctness, and the headline the course quotes.

Now the number that headline hides. Summed across the ten-question session, routed spends 5,644 tokens against naive's 16,948 — 3.0x, not 7.1x. The two aggregation cells are 64% of the router's entire session bill. A median is a fine summary of a typical question and a poor summary of a session, and the honest scorecard reports both.

Last: the routing table is itself a derived fact, so U11's law applies to it. Re-measure the grid — new seed, new mode implementation, new model — and re-derive the table, or the router keeps optimising for a world that no longer exists.
steps.youDo: Ask all ten presets in routed mode and add up the session strip; compare the total to the median you were quoted.
